::: {.lead}
The last island of *Lucky Raft* has treasure rooms. A door opens with a sum
of 10 or more, but the first die already shows a 6: are the chances still
1/6? Two storm cards in a row are rarer when the first card stays out of
the deck. A loot crate gives 100, 20 or 5 coins: what is it worth "on
average", and is a price of 25 coins fair? In lecture 20 you computed
probabilities by counting. In this lesson you use what you **already know**
(conditional probability), you multiply along branches that change, and you
compute the **expected value**, the most important number for the balance of
a game with chance. Every section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary conditional-probability dependent-events independent-events multiplication-rule tree-diagram random-variable expected-value fair-game >}}

## 21.1 Conditional probability

Sometimes part of the result is already known. Then the sample space gets
smaller (@fig-cond).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 21.1 — Conditional probability"}
The probability of A when we know that B happened is
$$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(B)}.$$
With equally likely outcomes: count the outcomes of A **only inside B**,
and divide by the number of outcomes of B.
:::

![P(A | B): count only inside B.](images/conditional-grid.png){#fig-cond width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 21.1 — The first die is a 6"}
The door opens with a sum of 10 or more (A). Before the roll, P(A) = 6/36 =
1/6.

1. The first die shows 6 (B): only (6,1), …, (6,6) are left, 6 outcomes.
2. Sums of 10 or more among them: (6,4), (6,5), (6,6): 3 outcomes.
3. P(A | B) = 3/6 = **1/2**. Knowing B made A three times more likely.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 21.2 — At least one 6, and a double"}
B = at least one 6: 11 outcomes. A = a double: inside B only (6,6).
P(A | B) = 1/11, while P(A) = 6/36 = 1/6.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/conditional-lab.html" poster="sims/conditional-lab.png" title="Conditional Lab: what do we know already?" height="740" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Dividing by all 36 outcomes after the condition. The condition removes the
outcomes outside B: divide by the number of outcomes in B.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Count inside B"}
Two dice. Find (a) P(sum 7 | first die is 1); (b) P(a double | the sum is
even); (c) P(sum 10 or more | at least one 6). Check one in **Conditional
Lab**.

*Your result:* three probabilities.
:::

## 21.2 Dependent events and the multiplication rule

In lecture 20 two draws were independent because the card went back. When
it stays out, the second branch changes (@fig-tree).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 21.2 — The multiplication rule"}
For any two events,
$$P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B \mid A).$$
Events are **dependent** when the first result changes the chances of the
second (drawing without putting back). In a tree diagram, each branch after
the first step has a **conditional** probability.
:::

![Two cards without putting the first back.](images/tree-no-return.png){#fig-tree width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 21.3 — Two storms in a row"}
12 event cards, 3 storms. A player draws two cards and keeps the first.

1. P(first storm) = 3/12.
2. After a storm, 11 cards are left with 2 storms: P(second storm | first
   storm) = 2/11.
3. P(two storms) = 3/12 × 2/11 = 6/132 = **1/22**, rarer than 1/16 with the
   card put back.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using 3/12 again for the second card. Without putting back, both the number
of storms and the number of cards change.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A deck of quests"}
A deck has 10 quest cards: 4 easy, 6 hard. Draw two without putting back.
Find P(two easy) and P(one easy, then one hard).

*Your result:* two probabilities.
:::

## 21.3 Independent or not?

Knowing B can change A, or not. This gives a clear test for independence.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 21.3 — Independence"}
A and B are **independent** when
$$P(A \mid B) = P(A),$$
that is, when knowing B does not change A. Then P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 21.4 — Two tests"}
1. A = second die is 6, B = first die is 6: P(A | B) = 1/6 = P(A).
   **Independent:** the dice do not talk to each other.
2. A = sum 10 or more, B = first die is 6: P(A | B) = 1/2 ≠ 1/6.
   **Dependent.**
3. Storm cards without putting back: P(2nd storm | 1st storm) = 2/11 ≠ 3/12.
   **Dependent.**
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"After three misses, a hit must come." For independent events, like rolls
of a die, the past does not change the next roll. (In lecture 25 you see
how games handle this feeling.)
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Test"}
Two dice. Are these independent? (a) A = a double, B = first die is 1;
(b) A = sum 7, B = first die is 6; (c) A = sum 12, B = first die is 6.

*Your result:* three answers with P(A | B) and P(A).
:::

## 21.4 Random variables and the expected value

Games give rewards: coins, damage, points. A number that depends on chance
is a **random variable**, and its long-run average is the **expected value**
(@fig-ev).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 21.4 — Expected value"}
A **random variable** X takes the values x₁, x₂, … with the probabilities
p₁, p₂, … Its **expected value** is
$$E(X) = x_1 p_1 + x_2 p_2 + \dots$$
E is the average per try over many tries; a single try usually gives a
different value.
:::

![The expected value of a loot crate.](images/expected-value.png){#fig-ev width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 21.5 — The loot crate"}
Gold 100 coins (1/10), silver 20 coins (3/10), wood 5 coins (6/10):

1. E = 100 · 0.1 + 20 · 0.3 + 5 · 0.6 = 10 + 6 + 3 = **19 coins**.
2. The plain average (100 + 20 + 5) / 3 ≈ 41.7 is wrong: wood comes far more
   often than gold.
3. A player who opens 100 crates gets about 1900 coins.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 21.6 — Damage of a sword"}
A hit does 10 damage; with probability 0.2 it is a critical hit of 25.
E = 10 · 0.8 + 25 · 0.2 = 8 + 5 = 13 damage per hit.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/crate-lab.html" poster="sims/crate-lab.png" title="Crate Lab: the expected value of a loot crate" height="800" >}}

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
float ExpectedCoins(int[] coins, float[] p) {
    float e = 0f;
    for (int i = 0; i < coins.Length; i++) e += coins[i] * p[i];
    return e;   // 100, 20, 5 with 0.1, 0.3, 0.6 → 19
}
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Forgetting to check that the probabilities add up to 1. If they do not, an
outcome is missing or counted twice.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Two crates"}
1. In **Crate Lab**, open 1000 crates and compare the average with E = 19.
2. Compute E for a crate with gold 50 (2/10), silver 20 (3/10) and wood 0
   (5/10).

*Your result:* an average and one E.
:::

## 21.5 Fair games and the number of tries

The expected value tells a designer whether a game of chance takes or
gives coins, and how long players wait for a rare item (@fig-fair).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 21.5 — Fair game and expected tries"}
The **expected gain** of a game is E(win) − price. A game is **fair** when
the expected gain is 0. If one try succeeds with probability p, the
**average number of tries** until the first success is **1/p**.
:::

![A fair price and the average number of tries.](images/fair-game.png){#fig-fair width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 21.7 — The dice stand"}
Pay 2 coins, roll a die, a 6 wins 10 coins.

1. E(win) = 10 · 1/6 ≈ 1.67 coins.
2. Expected gain = 1.67 − 2 ≈ **−0.33** coins per game: the stand wins in
   the long run.
3. A fair price would be 10/6 ≈ 1.67 coins.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 21.8 — Waiting for gold"}
Gold comes with p = 1/10: on average 10 crates. With p = 1/50 it is 50
crates; many players will need 100 or more, and some will give up. This is
why designers check both E and 1/p.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"With p = 1/10, the 10th crate surely has gold." 1/p is an average: after 10
crates, about 35 % of the players still have no gold (0.9¹⁰ ≈ 0.35).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Fair or not?"}
A spinner has 8 equal parts; one part wins 20 coins. A spin costs 3 coins.
(a) Is it fair? (b) Which price is fair? (c) How many spins on average until
a win?

*Your result:* three answers.
:::

## 21.6 Decisions with expected value

Players and designers compare choices by their expected values, and also
by their risk (@fig-choice).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 21.6 — Choosing with E"}
To compare choices, compute E for each one. A higher E is better **on
average**. The **risk** is how far single results are from E: a choice with
the same E but more extreme results is riskier.
:::

![Two chests with different expected values and risks.](images/ev-choice.png){#fig-choice width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 21.9 — The safe and the risky chest"}
1. Safe chest: always 50 coins, E = 50.
2. Risky chest: 120 coins with probability 1/2, else 0: E = 60.
3. The risky chest is better on average, but half of the players get
   nothing. A designer might add a small prize (20 coins) instead of 0 so
   that no player leaves with nothing: E = 120 · 0.5 + 20 · 0.5 = 70.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Looking only at the best result ("120 coins!"). Compare the expected values,
and then think about the risk for the player.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Choose"}
Option A: 30 coins for sure. Option B: 100 coins with probability 0.25, else
10 coins. Compute both E and say which one you would put in a game for new
players, and why.

*Your result:* two expected values and one sentence.
:::

## Case study: Treasure Odds

The treasure rooms of *Lucky Raft*: a door when the first die is already a
6, two storm cards without putting back, a loot crate with gold, silver and
wood, a dice game with a price of 2 coins, a golden key with a drop chance of
1/20, and a choice between a safe and a risky chest. The Game challenge of
the interactive lesson uses these rooms. In the mini-game below you choose
the right probability or expected value in each room.

## Further reading

Rosen, *Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications*, 8th ed., Sections 7.2
(conditional probability, independence) and 7.4 (expected value). Schell,
*The Art of Game Design*, 3rd ed., Chapter 12 (expected value in game
design).

## Exercises

1. Two dice, the first is 3. P(sum 7)?
2. Two dice, the sum is 8. P(a double)?
3. Write the formula of P(A | B).
4. Draw two cards from 10 cards with 2 jokers, without putting back. P(two
   jokers)?
5. The same with putting back. P(two jokers)?
6. Are two rolls of a die independent? Why?
7. A = first die is even, B = sum 7. Are A and B independent?
8. X is 4 with p = 0.5, 0 with p = 0.3 and 10 with p = 0.2. E(X)?
9. A crate: 200 coins (1/20), 10 coins (19/20). E?
10. Why is the plain average of the values not the expected value?
11. Pay 5 coins; win 30 coins with p = 1/8. Expected gain?
12. Which price makes the game of exercise 11 fair?
13. A rare pet drops with p = 1/25. How many tries on average?
14. With p = 1/10, what part of the players has no gold after 10 crates?
15. Safe: 40 coins. Risky: 100 coins with p = 0.3, else 10. Which has the
    higher E?
16. Why may a designer not choose the option with the highest E for new
    players?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. 1/6 (only (3,4)).
2. 1/5 ((2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2): one double).
3. P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B).
4. 2/10 × 1/9 = 1/45.
5. 2/10 × 2/10 = 1/25.
6. Yes: the first roll does not change the second.
7. P(A | B) = 3/6 = 1/2 = P(A): yes, independent.
8. 4 · 0.5 + 0 + 10 · 0.2 = 4.
9. 200/20 + 10 · 19/20 = 10 + 9.5 = 19.5.
10. The values have different probabilities.
11. 30/8 − 5 = 3.75 − 5 = −1.25 coins.
12. 3.75 coins.
13. 25.
14. 0.9¹⁰ ≈ 0.35, about 35 %.
15. Risky: 100 · 0.3 + 10 · 0.7 = 37 < 40, so the safe one.
16. A high E with a high risk can leave many new players with nothing.
:::
